# Audio fixtures

Generated by `scripts/generate_audio_fixtures.py` — run it again any time to regenerate these
byte-for-byte (Piper's inference is deterministic given the same model, text and flags).

| File | What it's for | Actual duration |
|---|---|---|
| `clean_utterance_3s.wav` | Baseline: one clean utterance, no silence in the middle | ~3.5s |
| `mid_sentence_pause_700ms.wav` | Endpointing: two phrases separated by an exact 700ms silence gap | ~3.4s |
| `accented_utterance.wav` | ASR robustness: British English (`en_GB-alan-medium`), distinct from the two US voices used elsewhere | ~5.0s |
| `silence_2s.wav` | VAD: pure digital silence, no speech at all | 2.00s |

All four are 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM — the frozen capture contract (`AUDIO_SAMPLE_RATE` /
`AUDIO_CHANNELS` / `AUDIO_SAMPLE_FORMAT` in `.env.example`).

## These are synthesized, not recorded

`docs/phase-0-LEARN.md` says to record these yourself now rather than mid-debug in Phase 1.
There's no microphone in the environment these were built in, so they're Piper TTS output
instead of real speech — a defensible stand-in for exercising the pipeline mechanically (VAD
triggers, endpointing timing, ASR runs at all), but **not** a substitute for real speech before
tuning VAD thresholds or endpointing silence windows against actual users. Piper audio is
cleaner than real speech: no breath noise, no room tone, no disfluency, near-perfect
diction. Endpointing tuned only against these will be optimistic.

**Before Phase 1 day 5's boundary-labelling work, replace or supplement these with real
recordings** — ideally including genuinely accented speech from a real speaker, not a second
synthetic voice standing in for one.
